title: A Storm Uncovered a Village Older Than the Pyramids
tags: skara brae, orkney, scotland, neolithic, archaeology
script: In 1850, a violent storm stripped the earth from a mound in Orkney, Scotland. Underneath were stone houses. Skara Brae is a Neolithic village about five thousand years old, first lived in before Stonehenge or Egypt's great pyramids were built. Inside, the furniture is still there: stone dressers, box beds, hearths, even drains under the floors. It's the best preserved Neolithic settlement in Western Europe. It took a storm to open the door.

title: He Sold 1.5 Million Plain Rocks as Pets
tags: pet rock, fads, 1970s, marketing
script: In 1975, a man sold ordinary rocks for about four dollars each, and nearly one and a half million people bought one. Advertising executive Gary Dahl created the Pet Rock. Each came in a cardboard box built like a pet carrier, complete with breathing holes and a bed of straw. Inside was a tongue in cheek manual on caring for your new companion. The craze lasted about six months. Easiest pet you'll ever own.

title: Julius Caesar Demanded a Bigger Ransom
tags: julius caesar, pirates, ancient rome, ransom
script: When pirates kidnapped Julius Caesar, he told them his ransom was too low. Around 75 BC, a young Caesar was seized at sea. The pirates asked for twenty talents of silver. Caesar insisted on fifty. During his thirty-eight days as a captive, he wrote poems and speeches and made the pirates listen. He also joked that he would come back and punish them all. They laughed. After his release, he raised a fleet and did exactly that.

title: A Whole Roman Legion Disappeared From History
tags: ninth legion, roman empire, roman britain, mystery
script: An entire Roman legion seems to have marched straight out of history. The Ninth Legion is last recorded in Britain in 108 AD, on a stone inscription at York. After about 120 AD, it disappears from surviving records. By the late second century, it's missing from official lists of Roman legions. Was it wiped out in a British revolt? Or moved to the Rhine and lost somewhere else? Historians still argue. Nobody knows how the Ninth ended.

title: A Baby Bird Flew 8,400 Miles Without Stopping
tags: bar-tailed godwit, birds, migration, record
script: In 2022, a five-month-old bird flew from Alaska to Tasmania without stopping once. It was a bar-tailed godwit wearing a tiny satellite tag. It took off from Alaska on October 13th and crossed the Pacific Ocean for eleven straight days. No landing. No eating. No rest. It covered at least 13,560 kilometers, about 8,400 miles, setting a world record for nonstop bird flight. It arrived having lost about half its weight. Its first migration ever.

title: Andrew Jackson's 1,400-Pound Cheese Party
tags: andrew jackson, big cheese, white house, 1837, presidents
script: In 1837, the White House opened its doors to the public for a giant cheese. President Andrew Jackson had been given a wheel weighing about fourteen hundred pounds by a New York dairy farmer. It sat in the White House for over a year, ripening. So Jackson invited everyone in Washington to help eat it. Crowds poured in. The entire cheese vanished in about two hours. The smell, reportedly, lingered for months.

title: Teenagers Found a Cave Full of Ice Age Art
tags: lascaux, cave paintings, france, prehistoric art, archaeology
script: In September 1940, teenagers in southwestern France squeezed through a hole in a hillside. Their lamps lit up walls covered in painted horses, bulls and stags. Lascaux holds nearly six thousand figures, made at least seventeen thousand years ago. After it opened to tourists, crowds brought heat, moisture and carbon dioxide that damaged the art. In 1963 it closed. Today visitors tour a full-scale replica. The original rests in the dark.

title: The Fax Machine Is Older Than the Telephone
tags: fax machine, inventions, telegraph, technology history
script: The fax machine is older than the telephone. In 1843, Scottish clockmaker Alexander Bain patented a way to copy images over telegraph wires, using synchronized pendulums to scan a message line by line. Then an Italian priest and physicist, Giovanni Caselli, built the pantelegraph. In 1865, it began commercial service between Paris and Lyon. That was about eleven years before the telephone arrived in 1876. Faxing came first.

title: The Year Ten Days Vanished From the Calendar
tags: gregorian calendar, 1582, pope gregory, timekeeping
script: In October 1582, ten days simply disappeared. People in Spain, Portugal, Italy and Poland went to bed on October fourth and woke up on October fifteenth. Why? The old Julian calendar ran slightly too long, and over centuries it had drifted away from the seasons, throwing off the date of Easter. Pope Gregory the Thirteenth fixed it by deleting ten days. Not everyone joined in. Britain and its American colonies waited until 1752.

title: A Clay Disc From Crete That No One Can Read
tags: phaistos disc, ancient crete, undeciphered, minoans
script: In 1908, archaeologists on Crete dug up a clay disc that no one alive can read. It came from the ruins of the Minoan palace at Phaistos. Both sides carry a spiral of picture signs, 45 different symbols in all. Each sign was pressed in with a stamp before the clay was fired, a kind of ancient typesetting. It was likely made in the Bronze Age, over 3,000 years ago. Many have offered translations. None is accepted.

title: Lightning Is Hotter Than the Surface of the Sun
tags: lightning, weather, physics, storms
script: A lightning bolt can be about five times hotter than the surface of the Sun. Lightning is simply electric charge on the move. But air is a poor conductor, and as that current forces its way through, the air heats to around fifty thousand degrees Fahrenheit. When lightning hits a tree, the heat can flash the water in its sap into steam, sometimes bursting the tree or peeling off its bark. The Sun has nothing on a thunderstorm.

title: A Booth Once Saved Lincoln's Son's Life
tags: robert todd lincoln, edwin booth, coincidence, civil war era, lincoln
script: Abraham Lincoln's son was once saved by a man named Booth. In 1863 or 1864, Robert Lincoln stood on a crowded train platform in Jersey City when the train began to move. He was twisted off his feet and slipped toward the gap. A stranger grabbed his coat collar and pulled him to safety. Robert recognized him: the famous actor Edwin Booth. Not long after, Edwin's brother, John Wilkes Booth, killed President Lincoln.

title: The Ghost Ship Buried in an English Field
tags: sutton hoo, anglo saxon, ship burial, england, archaeology
script: The ship had rotted away, but its shape was still printed in the sand. In 1939, on Edith Pretty's land in Suffolk, England, self-taught excavator Basil Brown found iron rivets still in place inside a burial mound. They traced a ship nearly ninety feet long. Its burial chamber held a famous helmet, a sword, gold and silver. It was an Anglo-Saxon royal burial, possibly King Raedwald's. The wood was gone. The ship remained.

title: Edison's Talking Doll Was a Total Flop
tags: thomas edison, failed inventions, dolls, phonograph
script: In 1890, Thomas Edison built a doll that could talk, and it was a disaster. Inside its body sat a tiny phonograph. Turn a crank, and it recited a nursery rhyme. Young women recorded the rhymes one doll at a time. But the wax records broke easily, the sound was poor, and dolls cost ten to twenty dollars. Edison pulled them within weeks. He reportedly called them his little monsters. Even geniuses miss sometimes.

title: Ancient Rome's Favorite Sauce Was Fermented Fish
tags: garum, ancient rome, roman food, history of food
script: Ancient Rome's favorite condiment was made from fish guts left out in the sun for months. It was called garum. Fish and salt sat in vats until they fermented into a salty, savory liquid, and Romans used it on everything, like ketchup. Factories were built far from towns because of the smell. Cheap versions fed soldiers, while luxury grades cost a fortune. Its flavor? Probably a lot like the fish sauce in your kitchen today.

title: Easter Island's Script That Nobody Can Read
tags: rongorongo, easter island, rapa nui, undeciphered
script: On one of the most remote islands on Earth, people carved a script nobody can read today. It's called rongorongo, from Easter Island, or Rapa Nui. Fewer than 30 wooden objects with these glyphs survive. To read it, you flip the tablet upside down at the end of every line. In 2024, scientists dated one tablet's wood to the 1400s, before Europeans arrived. But the last people who might have read it are long gone.

title: Saturn Could Float in Water. Sort Of.
tags: saturn, planets, space, density
script: Saturn is so light for its size that it could float in water. Well, almost. Saturn is about ninety-five times more massive than Earth, but it's made mostly of hydrogen and helium. Its average density is about 0.69 grams per cubic centimeter. Water is one. So on paper, it's lighter than bathwater. You'd just need a tub wider than the planet itself. And in reality, it would fall apart. Still, it's the only planet less dense than water.

title: The 1904 Olympic Marathon Was a Total Disaster
tags: 1904 olympics, marathon, st louis, sports history, olympics
script: The 1904 Olympic marathon may be the strangest race ever run. In St. Louis, runners faced ninety-degree heat and choking dust, with water at only one well. The first man across the finish line had ridden about ten miles in a car. He was disqualified. The real winner, Thomas Hicks, was given strychnine and brandy by his trainers. Another runner ate rotten apples and stopped for a nap. He still finished fourth.

title: This Pennsylvania Town Has Been Burning Since 1962
tags: centralia, mine fire, pennsylvania, ghost town, abandoned places
script: There's a town in Pennsylvania where the ground has been burning for more than sixty years. In 1962, a fire at Centralia's landfill likely spread into abandoned coal mines underneath. It never went out. Smoke seeped from cracks and basements. The state condemned the buildings, and most residents were bought out. Over a thousand people once lived here. The 2020 census counted five. And the fire is still burning below.

title: The Chess Robot That Fooled Napoleon
tags: mechanical turk, hoaxes, chess, automaton
script: In 1770, a chess playing machine stunned Europe. Wolfgang von Kempelen unveiled a turbaned mechanical figure seated at a wooden cabinet for Empress Maria Theresa. For decades the Turk toured and defeated challengers, reportedly including Benjamin Franklin and Napoleon. Audiences were shown whirring gears inside. But hidden in the cabinet sat a human chess master, moving pieces from below. It was the world's most famous fake robot.

title: Gladiators Were Basically Vegetarian
tags: gladiators, ancient rome, roman diet, archaeology
script: Roman gladiators were mostly vegetarian. Scientists studied bones from a gladiator cemetery in Ephesus, in modern Turkey, and found their diet was largely meat-free. They ate beans and grains, which is why Romans nicknamed them barley men. Even stranger, their bones contained unusually high levels of strontium. That fits ancient accounts of a drink made from plant ashes, taken after training to strengthen the body. The toughest fighters in Rome were carb-loading and drinking ash.

title: The Ghost Ship Story That May Be Completely Fake
tags: ourang medan, ghost ship, legend, sea mystery
script: The creepiest ghost ship story ever told might be about a ship that never existed. The legend says that in the late 1940s, a Dutch freighter called the Ourang Medan sent a chilling message: I die. Rescuers supposedly boarded and found no one alive. Then fire broke out and the ship sank. But researchers found no record of it in Lloyd's Register, or anywhere else. Even the rescue ship's logs show nothing. So who invented it?

title: Sharks Are Older Than Trees
tags: sharks, evolution, prehistoric, nature
script: Sharks are older than trees. The earliest evidence of sharks, a handful of tiny fossil scales, dates back around 450 million years. The first trees didn't appear until roughly 385 million years ago. That means for tens of millions of years, sharks were cruising the oceans of a planet with no forests at all. Since then, they've survived multiple mass extinctions. Dinosaurs came and went. Sharks are still here. Respect the original survivors.

title: The Brown Bear Who Joined the Polish Army
tags: wojtek, soldier bear, world war two, polish army, animals in war
script: During World War Two, a brown bear served with the Polish army. Polish soldiers adopted him as a cub in Iran in 1942 and named him Wojtek. To get him aboard a ship that banned mascots, they listed him as a private. He wrestled the men, drank beer, and rode in their trucks. Legend says he carried artillery shells in battle, though historians debate that. His unit made it their emblem anyway.

title: The Diamond Town the Desert Swallowed
tags: kolmanskop, namibia, ghost town, diamonds, abandoned places
script: In 1908, a railway worker in the Namib Desert spotted a shiny stone. It was a diamond. Soon Kolmanskop became a little German-style town in the sand, with an ice factory, a hospital, a casino and a skittle alley. But the diamonds ran thin, and richer fields were found farther south. By 1956, the town was completely abandoned. Then the dunes moved in. Today, sand fills its houses up to visitors' knees.

title: The Famous Potato Chip Origin Story Is a Myth
tags: potato chips, food myths, myth busting, snack history
script: You've probably heard how potato chips were invented. In 1853, a fussy customer at a Saratoga Springs restaurant kept sending back his fried potatoes, so chef George Crum sliced them paper thin out of spite. Some versions say the customer was Cornelius Vanderbilt. But Vanderbilt was in Europe at the time. And a recipe for potatoes fried in thin shavings appeared in an English cookbook back in 1817. Great story. Wrong origin.

title: The French King Who Thought He Was Made of Glass
tags: charles vi, medieval france, glass delusion, kings
script: A king of France reportedly believed his body was made of glass. Charles the Sixth ruled in the late 1300s and suffered serious bouts of mental illness. During some episodes, accounts say, he was terrified he would shatter. He would sit motionless for hours, wrapped in thick blankets, and wore clothing reinforced with iron rods to protect himself. He may be the first recorded case of what is now called the glass delusion, later seen across Europe.

title: A Schooner Ran Aground With Every Sailor Missing
tags: carroll a deering, ghost ship, outer banks, mystery
script: In 1921, a five-masted schooner ran aground off North Carolina with its sails set and not a single person aboard. The Carroll A. Deering was spotted stuck on the shoals near Cape Hatteras on January 31. Its lifeboats were gone. So were the log and the navigation gear. Days earlier, a lightship keeper had seen the crew on deck. Pirates? Mutiny? Rum-runners? Five government departments investigated. They never found an answer, or the crew.

title: This Salamander Can Regrow Parts of Its Brain
tags: axolotl, regeneration, animals, biology
script: This smiling salamander can regrow parts of its own brain. The axolotl lives wild in just one place, the canals and lake of Xochimilco in Mexico City. It keeps its feathery baby gills for life. Lose a leg? It grows a new one. It can also rebuild pieces of its heart, its spinal cord, and even sections of its brain, all without scarring. Scientists study it to learn how regeneration works. Sadly, it's critically endangered in the wild.

title: Sergeant Stubby, the Dog Who Went to WWI
tags: sergeant stubby, world war one, war dog, smithsonian, animals in war
script: One of America's most famous World War One veterans was a little dog. His name was Stubby. Private Robert Conroy smuggled him onto a troop ship to France. Stubby served with the 102nd Infantry through seventeen battles. After being hurt by mustard gas, he learned to warn soldiers when gas was coming. Back home, he met three presidents. Today, Stubby is preserved and displayed at the Smithsonian in Washington.
